summaries.summary: Language structure enables linguistic generalization beyond training distribution probability, allowing understanding of structurally valid utterances such as length 100 sentences.
Seq2seq-attention models perform well on standard datasets and capture some linguistic structure but remain brittle on uncharacteristic inputs.
High-capacity models may learn structure, but linguistic generalization requires avoiding overfitting to training-specific patterns and may be difficult to find.
The work trains seq2seq-attention models on a symbol replacement task and finds linguistic generalization highly sensitive to random seed changes.
A simple formal task eases analysis by mimicking input-output symbol alignments and local syntactic properties in translation, tagging and summarization.
The task rewrites each input symbol as k symbols from its associated output alphabet, requiring alignments and local syntactic conditions.
An example defines X, Y_A, Y_B, k=3, 48 possible permutations, random valid outputs, and output alphabets of size 16.
Models are single layer unidirectional seq2seq LSTMs with bilinear attention, vanilla SGD, a 2000-sample validation set, and hidden and embedding size 32.
A 5000-sample uncharacteristic validation set tuned learning rate and dropout to 0.125 and 0.1, with all other hyperparameters also decided using it.
Models were trained on 100,000 samples with lengths 5-10 and no repeated symbols to test generalization to repeats and different lengths.
Evaluation trained 50 models with different random seeds and created 4 test sets of 2000 samples: Standard, Repeat, Short, and Long.
Across 50 seeds, standard accuracy exceeded 99%, while deviations reached 13.39 for Repeat and 20.63 for Long, with highest nonstandard average 79.52%.
Table 4 gives summary statistics across all 50 runs, and Table 3 shows performances for individual random seeds.
Related work investigates RNNs capturing language generalization properties, context free and context sensitive languages, and hierarchical natural language syntax.
Prior work questions systematicity, notes difficulty generalizing to longer strings, and finds small amounts of longer training strings can help.
Generalization depends on random seed, which affects network initialization and training sample order, with BIBREF18 emphasizing presentation order.
Random seed variability in generalization despite stable standard test performance may motivate a new NLP evaluation paradigm emphasizing uncharacteristic structurally sound inputs.
